articles.title: Toward a novel framework of understanding the relationship between social media use and political knowledge: a systematic literature review
articles.authors: Cato Waeterloos, Desiree Schmuck, Peter Van Aelst, Michaël Opgenhaffen
articles.abstract: While recent quantitative research finds little evidence that citizens learn about politics from social media, it is unclear whether studies adequately capture platform complexity and often fragmented understandings of political knowledge. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically reviewed 78 papers that assess the quantitative association between social media use and political knowledge. Our critical assessment of how such studies conceptualize and operationalize social media use and political knowledge revealed a dual mismatch. First, social media use is often measured via general frequency, overlooking specific content (beyond “news”), actors (e.g., influencers), platforms (beyond Facebook/Twitter), and exposure modes (e.g., incidental). Second, knowledge measures remain conservative, focusing on institutional facts while neglecting issue-specific and noninstitutional topics. We propose a novel 3-dimensional framework and methodological pathways to address key limitations in the dominant normative tradition of studying the relationship between social media and political learning.

content.journal_full: Convergence: The International Journal of Research into New Media Technologies

articles.title: Podcast talk: Knowledge-making through voice, circulation, and listening
articles.abstract: This article argues that podcasting should be understood not merely as a means of disseminating knowledge, but as a knowledge-making practice in its own right. Drawing on theories of broadcast talk, mediated address, and communication as dissemination, it develops the concept of podcast talk to examine how podcasts organise knowledge through voice, sequence, intimacy, circulation, and listening. Rather than presenting a bounded empirical case study, the article synthesises existing podcast scholarship on narrative nonfiction, independent podcasting, journalism, counterpublics, intimacy, host authority, and listening contexts. It identifies three ways podcasting produces knowledge. First, by circulating voices and accounts through platforms and publics. Second, by reshaping expertise and authority through vocal presence, lived experience, and relational trust. Third, by making knowledge meaningful through embodied, affective listening encounters. At the same time, the article treats podcasting as an ambivalent epistemic form, whose intimacy and authority can also intensify misplaced trust, misinformation, and unequal visibility. Podcasting moves knowledge off the page by making communicative form central to knowledge-making practice.

articles.title: Expanded documentary and immersive technologies: Ludic logics and heritage mediation in ARTE’s interactive experiences
articles.abstract: This article examines the transformation of contemporary documentary practices through immersive and interactive technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality and game-based narrative structures. Positioned within debates on media convergence, the study argues that expanded documentary forms do not merely hybridise non-fiction with entertainment but reconfigure documentary epistemology through embodied immersion, procedural authorship and guided participation. Drawing on theories of expanded cinema, interactive documentary and game studies, the article clarifies the concept of ludic logics and distinguishes it from gamification and serious games. A qualitative comparative analysis of emblematic immersive documentary projects is conducted using a shared analytical grid focused on immersion, agency, narrative organisation and ethical positioning. The findings show that immersive non-fiction fosters situated and affective forms of knowledge while introducing new tensions between agency and authorial control. The article contributes to documentary and media convergence studies by providing a conceptually precise and methodologically replicable framework for analysing immersive non-fiction.

articles.title: Platform infrastructures of reading: Postliterary Attention Theory and summary-first interfaces
articles.abstract: Contemporary discourse frequently diagnoses an “attention crisis,” framing distraction and overload as individual or psychological failures. This article argues that the crisis is better understood as a transformation in the media-technological conditions of reading. It develops Postliterary Attention Theory (PLAT) to explain how platform infrastructures organise textual encounter through three mechanisms: pre-legibility, in which ranking and summary layers shape salience before reading; labour shift, in which platforms compress and pre-frame texts while readers inherit burdens of verification and contextual reconstruction; and temporal governance, in which refresh rhythms, notifications, and metric feedback normalise fragmented engagement. The outcome is stratified durational literacy: unequal capacity for sustained reading, interpretive depth, and visibility across different infrastructural and socioeconomic conditions. The article advances three propositions—attention as embodied media labour, algorithmic co-reading as hybrid literacy, and fragmentation as structural affect—and offers a conceptual demonstration of how PLAT may be operationalised through threshold analysis, with summary-first interfaces and AI-generated overviews treated as exemplary reading thresholds in discovery environments. It concludes by reframing media power as the organisation of literacy and by outlining a comparative agenda for studying reading under convergent media conditions.

articles.title: Kaleidoscopic contradictions: Ecological paradoxes in AI-powered interactive digital narrative
articles.abstract: This study aims to analyze the ecological contradictions inherent in artificial intelligence-supported interactive digital narrative systems. Drawing on theoretical frameworks such as post-digital aesthetics, media ecology, and critical environmental studies, the research analyzes case studies of interactive designs that question contradictory realities from perspectives including artificial intelligence and the environment, ecological media infrastructures, post-anthropocentric narratives, data criticism, and ethics. While praised for offering personalized and immersive narrative experiences, these works cause high environmental costs due to their reliance on unsustainable infrastructures. Although ecology-focused, they are mostly produced within technological systems that materially undermine this theme and are circulated through these systems. However, these material realities are often overshadowed by the visually impressive presentation of the narratives, leading to a new kind of ecological blindness. In this context, the contradictions of kaleidoscopic narratives in the creation of interactive art are questioned, and the importance of rethinking AI-supported digital narratives not only at the content level but also in terms of production and distribution infrastructures within an environmentally ethical context is discussed. The research offers suggestions on questions such as how to integrate design criticism and practice to reduce the energy costs of digital narrative and minimize its ecological impact, how to establish carbon-aware design methodologies and accountability frameworks, and how to incorporate environmental calculations into the production workflow, and it argues for the necessity of considering environmental costs as well as the need to move beyond a profit loss focused mindset as one of the most important problems of digital representation forms. Finally, calling for a new paradigm shift in the field of culture, the research emphasizes the importance of adopting eco-materialist paradigms, away from human-centeredness, for truly sustainable and ecologically sensitive digital narratives.

articles.title: Driving and Drivering
articles.abstract: Autonomous mobility does not invent distributed perception; it reorganises older relations among eye, body, vehicle and street into a predictive media infrastructure. Focussing on sensorised urban environments, this article theorises the post-ocular sensorium as a formation in which cameras, lidar, radar, V2X systems, digital twins and fleet memories convert the street into classifications, probabilities, alerts and trajectories. Through the cases of smart intersections, Chattanooga’s MLK Smart Corridor, autonomous-vehicle misclassification, routing anomalies and infrastructural error, the article examines how perception migrates from the driver’s eye to a lattice of vehicles, roadside instruments, municipal platforms and proprietary protocols. It argues that this migration produces not only new capacities for safety and anticipation, but also new forms of infrastructural illusion, in which model, map, message or feed slips out of register with the street it governs. The Chattanooga case is used to show that smart corridors are never merely technical prototypes: they inherit longer histories of urban planning, racialised displacement, pedestrian vulnerability and civic repair. The article therefore proposes Drivering as an ethics of acknowledgement for infrastructural seeing. Drivering names the civic discipline of making distributed road perception technically inspectable, publicly contestable, historically situated and ethically unfinished. Its conclusion is not a nostalgic recovery of human control, nor a refusal of machine perception, but a demand that networked sight remain answerable to the lives it classifies, anticipates and moves.

articles.title: Parent–Child Play and Media Addiction in Adolescence: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study
articles.authors: Chaeyun Lee, Hye In Jeong, Yeolib Kim
articles.abstract: Although media addiction is a recognized public health concern, the theoretical framework surrounding its longitudinal development remains relatively underdeveloped. This study addresses that gap by evaluating a developmental model that traces a path from early parent–child play at age 6 to adolescent media addiction at age 14, with executive function and peer attachment at age 10 examined as parallel mediators. We used three waves of data from a representative sample of 1,130 parent–child dyads in the Panel Study on Korean Children. Early parent–child play at age 6 significantly predicted higher executive function at age 10, which subsequently predicted lower media addiction at age 14. This indirect path via executive function was statistically significant. Conversely, the indirect effect through peer attachment was not significant, as peer attachment was unrelated to both early play and subsequent media addiction. The direct effect of parent–child play on adolescent media addiction was nonsignificant, demonstrating that the protective influence of early family play operates through cognitive mechanisms rather than social bonds. These findings shift the clinical focus from proximal adolescent factors to early prevention, emphasizing middle childhood as a critical therapeutic window for bolstering executive function to mitigate later media addiction risks.

articles.title: Internet Addiction Disorder and Cybersecurity Risk: A Neurobiological and Behavioral Review
articles.abstract: Internet addiction disorder (IAD) has attracted substantial clinical and scientific interest over the past two decades. Although the condition remains outside formal diagnostic frameworks in the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, accumulating neuroimaging evidence demonstrates that compulsive Internet use is associated with disruptions in dopaminergic reward circuitry and prefrontal cortical function that closely parallel those observed in substance use disorders. These neurobiological changes, encompassing impaired executive function, elevated impulsivity, and heightened reward sensitivity, may carry implications for cybersecurity. Available evidence suggests that individuals exhibiting addictive patterns of Internet use show reduced compliance with security protocols, increased vulnerability to social engineering, and elevated engagement in risky online behaviors, although directionality cannot be established with confidence given the predominantly cross-sectional evidence base. The present narrative review synthesizes evidence from addiction neuroscience, clinical psychology, and cybersecurity research to propose a mechanistic account of the IAD–cybersecurity risk relationship. The review identifies impaired prefrontal inhibitory control as the central neurobiological mediator linking IAD to cybersecurity vulnerability, mediated primarily through impulsivity and compounded by the attentional and affective characteristics that render addicted individuals susceptible to social engineering. Drawing on literature spanning 2017–2026, the review also situates this account within a contemporary regulatory context, including the documented acceleration of problematic Internet use during the COVID-19 pandemic, Australia’s landmark social media minimum age legislation, and an influential 2026 civil verdict in which a U.S. jury found major platform operators liable for harms arising from addictive design. Clinical, organizational, and policy implications are discussed.

articles.title: Digital Agency Tools: A Way to Buffer the Negative Effects of Excessive Phone Use?
articles.abstract: In times of ubiquitous smartphone use, most users adopt one or more self-imposed rules regarding their device usage, also known as voluntary digital disconnection. Drawing on the Integrative Model of Mobile Media Use and Need Experiences (IM³UNE), this study provides empirical evidence on the adoption of digital agency tools and their potential in mitigating ill-being (depression, anxiety, and stress) associated with excessive smartphone use. We conducted a quota-based online survey involving n = 384 ( M age = 49.6) smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium). The results provide a systematization of different digital agency tools, showing they are widely used among adults. Importantly, we provide preliminary evidence on their potential in buffering ill-being due to excessive smartphone use. For users of detox apps and in-app well-being features, the associations between excessive use and ill-being were nonsignificant, unlike for nonusers of these tools. For users of default device settings, such as iOS ScreenTime, there were no differences. Our findings contribute to theory by applying and empirically testing critical elements of the IM³UNE model. Empirically, our findings indicate the importance of studying different types of tools, as they do not appear to be equally beneficial.

articles.title: AI-Mediated Mental Health Support: The Role of Attachment Orientation and Psychological Distress
articles.authors: Dorit Hadar Shoval, Elad Refoua, Karny Gigi, Yuval Haber, Inbar Levkovich, Iftach Tsafrir, Ori Pen, Zohar Elyoseph
articles.abstract: General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are increasingly serving as quasi-social agents, representing a novel form of informal AI-mediated help-seeking. This study examined associations between adult attachment orientations (Experiences in Close Relationships-Relationship Structures questionnaire), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales–21), and the use of GenAI for mental health support. In a nonprobability sample of 584 Israeli adult GenAI users, 29.3 percent reported having turned to these models at least once for emotional support, coping advice, or mental health assistance; the proportion reached 47.0 percent among those reporting severe distress. These self-reported figures reflect any such contact, from a single exchange to sustained use. Hierarchical logistic regression identified distress as the strongest psychological correlate of use. Younger age and female gender predicted use. Attachment anxiety was associated with use, but this association did not remain significant once distress was included, a pattern consistent with the shared variance between the two constructs. Attachment avoidance was negatively but nonsignificantly associated with use. Findings position general-purpose GenAI as an accessible, low-barrier resource disproportionately used by distressed individuals. The high uptake among severely distressed users (47.0 percent) points to potential safety concerns and to a need for systematic evaluation of the safety, crisis-response quality, and clinical-displacement risks of consumer-facing AI use.

articles.title: The role of democratic values in shaping perceptions of political incivility in European liberal democracies
articles.abstract: This study investigates whether citizens’ perceptions of political incivility converge across liberal democracies and the extent to which individual orientations towards democracy and democratic values are associated with sensitivity to incivility. Drawing on a comparative survey conducted in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom ( N = 3500), it examines the individual factors associated with sensitivity to incivility. The results show that support for democracy and endorsement of democratic values are the most influential predictors of sensitivity to incivility, with higher levels associated with greater sensitivity, whereas anti-political attitudes are associated with lower sensitivity. These findings indicate that sensitivity to incivility is primarily associated with citizens’ orientations towards democracy and its normative principles rather than with national contextual differences. Citizens in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom assess incivility in remarkably similar ways, despite differences in electoral systems, media systems, and political cultures.

articles.title: The United States’ Strategic Political Communication and the Production of a Strategy Video Game “With an Authentic Iraqi Feel”
articles.abstract: This article deals with a unique case study that has never been studied before in which the U.S. Department of Defense funded the production and distribution of a strategy video game during its occupation of Iraq between 2003–2011. Using a freedom of information request, a number of unclassified documents were obtained by the author, which included details of vast media campaigns, including the production of a prodemocracy strategy video game. There was never any attribution of the real video game maker, allegedly to enhance its credibility among its Iraqi users. After obtaining the game from Iraq and surveying the literature on the use of video games by various militaries, I offer a critical assessment of the game itself, highlighting the ideals and values that the U.S. government wanted to emphasize in its concealed information operation to the Iraqi public. Using the theoretical framework of strategic political communication, I argue that the objective of this video game was to manufacture Iraqi citizens who believed in the democratic process and the rule of law, yet who could also indirectly serve the U.S. strategic interests in Iraq.

articles.title: Popular Pornographic Games on Steam
articles.abstract: This study examines which pornographic games are popular on Steam and identifies what players consider to be features of a good pornographic game. The analysis draws on Steam user reviews and genre folk taxonomy drawn from the f95zone database. Game popularity is determined by review scores and counts; these correlate with sales figures, and the combined review counts are used to map genre prevalence and popularity. Steam reviews and genre descriptors are analyzed using structural topic modeling to identify recurring patterns and content themes. The findings show that popular pornographic games on Steam predominantly follow heteronormative pornoscripts, centering male player perspectives and conventional sexual practices. At the same time, a subset of successful games foreground transgressive and taboo content, including monster sex. Across both patterns, pornographic conventions are closely integrated with established game and story conventions, particularly those of narrative-driven genres such as visual novels and role-playing games.

articles.title: Keeping Ms. Pac-Man Out of the Club: Pacmania, Video Game Magazines, and the Gendered Guardrails of Digital Worlds in the Early 1980s
articles.abstract: This article reveals a gendered backlash to the increased participation of female gamers during Pacmania in the United States in the early 1980s. As Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man gained immense national recognition, gaming magazines, newsletters, and newspaper articles recognized the female gamers who contributed to tournaments and gaming culture. However, some male gamers mocked “cute” games, coded to female gamers, that supposedly undermined the stature attached to “serious” games. Present throughout gaming media but epitomized in the gaming magazine VIDIOT , this set of male gamers mocked female gamers and cute games that somehow undeservedly encroached upon their digital domain. This antiPacmania backlash was an early historical moment in which male gamers and corporate institutions installed gendered guardrails to preserve video games as an exclusive realm that marginalized females. This moment was an early case study of the gendered ideals that shaped the next decades’ male-focused advertising and even Gamergate.

articles.title: When AI hurts the pros: expertise-fixation costs and platform deployment of generative AI in subscription markets
articles.authors: Zhiyong Li, Hongxin Liu, Shiyao Shan, Min Zhang, Qiuxiao Yang
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines when subscription-based content platforms should deploy generative AI, given the heterogeneous AI-induced Einstellung effects on novice and expert creators. It identifies conditions under which deployment improves or undermines platform performance. Design/methodology/approach A calibrated two-sided market model characterizes equilibrium outcomes under AI and non-AI regimes, derives closed-form deployment thresholds, and tests robustness to heterogeneous expert adoption and positive novice baseline quality. Findings AI deployment is governed by a cost threshold, with welfare effects depending on implementation costs and standalone utility for a consumer joining the platform. Low-cost deployment can benefit platforms, creators, and consumers, whereas high costs may reduce profitability and stakeholder welfare by amplifying expert-side cognitive friction. Maximizing AI adoption is therefore not always optimal, even when AI raises average productivity. Research limitations/implications The analysis treats creator quality as exogenous and considers only one platform. The core deployment logic nevertheless remains robust to heterogeneous expert adoption and positive novice baseline quality. Practical implications Before deployment, managers should assess the composition of creators, implementation costs, and consumer demand. Enhancing AI-workflow compatibility and using targeted strategies can reduce expert-side friction and expand the conditions under which AI creates ecosystem value. Social implications Indiscriminate AI deployment may discourage expert participation and reduce content quality and consumer welfare, despite increasing the overall content supply. Originality/value This study offers a cognition-aware deployment framework by incorporating heterogeneous creator responses into a two-sided market model. It identifies thresholds and welfare regimes showing when AI creates mutual gains and when strategic restraint is preferable.

articles.title: More, shorter, newer? How monetization reshapes creator strategy on YouTube Shorts
articles.authors: Soonjae Kwon, Kitae Kim, Sung-Hyuk Park
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines the causal impact of YouTube Shorts' ad-revenue sharing policy on creator production strategies in the short-form video creator economy. Design/methodology/approach Using 36,507 videos from 342 top global channels, we employ a regression discontinuity in time design. Computer vision techniques measure four attributes of each creator's production strategy: output volume, video length, editing pace, and content novelty. Findings The policy drove an immediate reduction in video length without expanding output volume, consistent with substitution toward cheaper per-unit configurations rather than output scaling. Entertainment creators shortened their videos most sharply, while informative creators slowed their editing pace to preserve comprehension. Long-type creators pursued per-unit cost reduction, while short-type creators invested in content novelty. Research limitations/implications The sample covers top-tier global channels, so emerging creators may respond differently. The findings show that the quantity-expansion result from low-marginal-cost user-generated content settings does not extend to high-marginal-cost production, where incentives reallocate effort within existing output rather than expand it. Practical implications A uniform monetization policy does not produce uniform outcomes. Incentive design should anticipate that creators adjust different production attributes depending on their content goals and capabilities. Originality/value This study provides causal evidence that performance-contingent monetization reshapes production strategy in a high-cost video production context and that one platform-wide policy generates different responses across creator types.

articles.title: IT professionals' alumni networks and firm innovation: the role of informal connections in dynamic environments
articles.authors: Binger Lin, Chunmian Ge, Junhui Jiang, Yichao Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose We aim to address a critical organizational challenge – how firms can leverage informal networks to enhance innovation in increasingly dynamic environments. Alumni networks connect IT professionals and support knowledge exchange across geographical and organizational boundaries, facilitating innovation through distributed collaboration. However, prior studies have inadequately examined whether and how alumni networks help IT professionals overcome boundary barriers and contribute to firm innovation. Our study fills this gap and offers practical implications for management policies. Design/methodology/approach Using data from a large online professional social networking platform, we construct alumni networks of IT professionals and use linear regression and Poisson models to examine their impact on firm innovation. This study also conducts several robustness tests, including reconstructing the alumni networks, adopting alternative centrality measures, applying different thresholds to identify high-centrality IT professionals and using lagged independent variables. Findings We find that firms with more IT professionals occupying central positions in the alumni network exhibit stronger innovation performance. Furthermore, this positive relationship is strengthened in conditions of high technological and market dynamism, highlighting the value of informal networks in driving innovation in dynamic environments. Originality/value The positive effect of IT professionals' alumni networks on firm innovation extends the understanding of informal networks by highlighting their significance in facilitating information access and integration across organizational boundaries. We further illustrate how the impact of alumni networks varies with environmental dynamism, offering practical insights into how firms can strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity in response to environmental uncertainty.

articles.title: Measuring consumer literacy about online fraud: effects on perceived financial risk and trust in online sellers
articles.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop and validate a scale to measure consumer literacy about online fraud (CLOF). While prior research has linked general education and financial literacy to fraud victimization, specific knowledge about online fraud remains underexplored. The CLOF scale addresses this gap by capturing consumers' awareness of fraud-related practices and protective behaviors. The study also examines the relationships between CLOF and perceived financial risk, trust in online sellers, and online buying intensity. Design/methodology/approach Following established scale development procedures, we conducted focus groups, item generation, Q-sort validation, and pilot testing. The CLOF scale was tested across three studies in the USA, Sweden, and the UK using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Reliability and validity were assessed through Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, AVE, and discriminant validity. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to test the hypotheses. Findings The CLOF scale comprises six dimensions (i.e. Knowledge about identity theft; Verification of the legitimacy of companies; Knowledge of how to report fraud; Checking red flags that prevent being a victim of online scams; Knowledge and use of tools that protect against scams; and Reading terms and conditions as a protection practice). The results also show that CLOF is negatively associated with perceived financial risk and positively associated with trust in online sellers. Originality/value Existing scales do not capture literacy about online fraud effectively, with inconsistent literacy–fraud relationships reported in the literature. Hence, there is an urgent need for effective measurement and associated behavior in this context. This research introduces the first validated scale specifically designed to measure consumer literacy about online fraud. The scale offers practical utility for scholars, policymakers, and practitioners aiming to enhance fraud prevention and consumer confidence in e-commerce.

articles.title: From scripted responses to emotional reactions: exploring customer incivility behavior and emotions during chatbot capability failures—a machine learning approach
articles.authors: Vida Siahtiri, Achini Adikari, Damminda Alahakoon
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines how chatbot capability failures lead to customers' incivility in AI-enabled service delivery through customers' emotional responses. It also investigates whether chatbot-expressed empathy, as a recovery-oriented capability, weakens or intensifies the relationship between customers' negative emotions and incivility. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on social response theory, we analyzed 32,586 text conversations from a university library chatbot using a framework that combines natural language processing and supervised machine learning to extract the constructs of interest. We then estimated a moderated mediation model using PROCESS to examine the proposed relationships. Findings The study identified chatbot capability failures and empathy, customer digital incivility and customer emotional profiles. The findings showed that technical and functional chatbot capability failures elicited negative customer emotions, and that these negative emotions fully mediated the relationship between chatbot capability failures and customer incivility behaviors. Although we anticipated that chatbot empathy, as a recovery-oriented capability, would mitigate the effect of negative emotions on incivility, the findings revealed the opposite: empathy strengthened rather than attenuated this effect. We termed this paradox the “empathy backfire,” indicating that empathic expressions alone were insufficient and could even intensify customer incivility when they were not matched by adequate chatbot capability. Originality/value The study advances social response theory by revealing a counterintuitive empathy backfire effect in which chatbot empathy intensifies, rather than mitigates, customer incivility behaviors. Although empathy often helps mitigate the negative effects of service failure on customer behavior in human interactions, managers should not assume that empathetic language embedded in chatbot scripts will produce comparable benefits.

articles.title: Inoculating against fatalistic beliefs: a comparative test of narrative and non-narrative strategies
articles.abstract: This study compares the effectiveness of narrative and non-narrative inoculation messages in reducing fatalistic beliefs and fostering resistance to conflicting cancer information. A two-phase randomized experiment (N = 572 in Phase 1; n = 332 in Phase 2) tested their effects on counterarguing against attack, cancer fatalism, perceived efficacy, and intentions to adopt cancer risk-reduction behaviors. Compared with control, both inoculation messages reduced cancer fatalism, enhanced perceived efficacy, and increased certain intentions to adopt certain risk-reduction behaviors. Narrative inoculation elicited more counterarguing against attack than the non-narrative counterpart. Inoculation effects also varied by baseline fatalism, functioning therapeutically by immediately reducing initially high fatalism and, more modestly, prophylactically by maintaining initially low fatalism. These findings extend inoculation theory by elucidating the role of message format in sustaining resistance to negative media effects, and by demonstrating the theory’s potential dual prophylactic–therapeutic functionality in a fatalistic belief context.

articles.title: Writing the Situated Self: Intersectional and Geographic Patterning in College Admissions Essays
articles.authors: AJ Alvero, anthony lising antonio, Leslie Luqueño, Francis Pearman
articles.abstract: Written language is often considered a reflection of the author's internal thoughts, states, and characteristics. This is why writing is used in evaluation to make inferences about authors, but also why social scientists use text as a lens into psychological states. We present a complementary perspective: that writing systematically reflects the social environments of authors. We explore these dynamics in a large corpus of college admissions essays ( n = 232,838 essays submitted by 76,510 self-identified Hispanic applicants from 2015 to 2017) and metadata about author sociodemographics, including the ZIP code of their high school, gender identity, and household income. We find that intersectional demographic markers are highly salient. We further demonstrate that ZIP code-level socioeconomic measures are strongly correlated with the writing style and content of local applicants. Finally, we show that misclassification rates vary geographically and are modestly associated with local demographic composition and social capital, indicating that writing is influenced both socially and geographically. By documenting strong alignment between text and authors that is observable through machine reading, our findings clarify how author demographics and context structure what is written and, stylistically, how. Framing text as an external, social process rather than purely internal creates opportunities to bridge psychological and sociological data, methods, and theories to better understand the connections between language and society, especially in moments of evaluation. Because these texts were produced before the popularization of large language models (LLMs), our results serve as useful benchmarks for archival work and also generate new questions as LLMs mediate written self-presentation.

articles.title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Human Narratives
articles.abstract: How can artificial intelligence (AI) best support human problem-solving, creativity, and group work? I introduce a psychological account of narrative agency that formalizes how human groups learn from, communicate, and influence narratives in digital contexts. I then discuss how AI models impact human performance through a narrative agency lens, from authoring better essays to finding consensus online. Crucially, AI outputs are routed through a human's narrative agency to generate a result that causes change in the world. Designing human–AI systems around maintaining people's narrative agency is therefore essential for human–AI alignment.

articles.title: Optimizing Naloxone Education
articles.abstract: Abstract: Message sensation is commonly used in educational messaging to capture attention, yet its impact on cognitive learning appears paradoxical. Drawing on the Activation Model of Information Exposure and the Limited Capacity Model of Motivated Mediated Message Processing, this study examines how message sensation influences memory and knowledge improvement. An in-person 2 (death imagery: absent vs. present) × 2 (sound effects: absent vs. present) × 2 (animation: talking-head vs. action) between-subjects experiment was conducted among 603 US adults. Path modeling revealed that the need for activation moderated the effects of perceived message sensation on visual encoding and retrieval: as this need decreased, the association between perceived message sensation and memory accuracy (visual encoding and retrieval) shifted from positive to negative. These findings advance media psychology by showing how message features and individual traits interact to shape learning in high-stakes public health contexts.

articles.title: Patterns in Mother-Child and Father-Child Mutually Responsive Orientation During Mealtimes: Correlation With Martial Satisfaction
articles.authors: Qiujie Gong, Samantha Iwinski, Sehyun Ju, Brent A. McBride, Kelly K. Bost
articles.abstract: Marital relationship and parent-child interaction have been found to be correlated. Using observational data from family mealtime interactions, this study examined mother-child and father-child mutually responsive orientation (MRO) among toddlers (18-24 months) during mealtime and its association with mother-reported marital satisfaction. MRO refers to a positive, reciprocal, and cooperative parent–child relationship that serves as a foundation for early socialization. Our final sample consisted of 71 families. Latent profile analysis identified a four-class solution. Class 1 reflected moderately high interaction quality for both father–child and mother–child relationships. Class 2 was characterized by moderate father–child interaction quality coupled with low mother–child interaction quality. Class 3 demonstrated comparatively lower father–child interaction quality and high mother–child interaction quality. Finally, Class 4 represented high-quality interactions for both fathers and mothers across domains. Findings further indicated that families characterized by lower-quality father–child interactions alongside higher-quality mother–child interactions reported the lowest levels of maternal marital satisfaction. In contrast, when fathers demonstrated moderate or high-quality interactions with their child, mothers reported higher marital satisfaction, regardless of the quality of mother–child interactions. These results underscore the importance of father–child interaction quality in shaping mothers’ perceptions of marital satisfaction.

articles.title: Watchdog Science Journalism: How Retraction Watch Fosters Accountability in Science
articles.abstract: Although science reporters have long been urged to adopt the role of the journalistic watchdog, scholars have not extensively examined how this role can be understood conceptually or in practice. This exploratory case study examines Retraction Watch, founded in 2010, as an illuminating example of watchdog science journalism that holds science to account around the epistemological claim, central to science’s cultural authority, that it is self-correcting. Drawing on a thematic analysis of interviews with senior staff at the site and scholars who study retractions, the study finds that the site has undertaken accountability journalism of the little-scrutinised phenomenon of retractions, has reported systematically on retractions, has questioned and determined the reasons for retractions, has created a database of retractions to aid science in its self-correction, and has provided knowledge-based journalism for its specialist public interested in scientific integrity. The article argues that Retraction Watch has expanded beyond journalism to operate as a novel journalistic hybrid institution that combines science journalism with the scientific infrastructure of its database, activities underpinned by a normative value of accountability. As a journalistic hybrid institution, it illustrates what future organisational forms of science journalism might look like.

articles.title: Journalism as Science’s Watchdog: The Vibrancy and Vulnerability of an Increasingly Diverse Ecosystem
articles.abstract: Watchdog science journalism, broadly understood, investigates, exposes, and warns society of the misuses and abuses of science methods, processes, outcomes, and authority by those practicing, funding, and/or using science in the public domain. Amid rising threats to research integrity, this thematic issue provides a first comprehensive set of empirical and conceptual insights into how this type of journalism is becoming both vibrant and vulnerable. It reveals that watchdog science journalism is recognized as essential by members of the public and by journalists alike and is empowered by an increasingly diverse set of actors, both within and beyond traditional journalism. Yet, ongoing challenges within and beyond the news industry are putting pressure on this role, undermining journalists’ capacity to effectively scrutinize and sound the alarm about research integrity problems that put the public interest at risk.

articles.title: African Community Media, AI, and the Question of Community Participation in the Disruptive Era
articles.authors: Lyton Ncube, Allen Munoriyarwa, Albert Chibuwe, Refilwe Whitney Mofokeng, Antonette Kakujaha-Murangi
articles.abstract: In this article, we examine the nexus of Southern African community newspapers’ sceptical AI integration and grassroots democracy. The sceptical approach to AI integration in marginalised media markets of Southern African community newspapers’ news ecosystems is interrogated. We respond to the questions: In what ways is the integration of AI tools in everyday news production routines within Southern African community media institutions defined by scepticism? What is the basis of scepticism amongst Southern African community media journalists? What are the implications for grassroots democracy in these communities? The Southern African community media under study are drawn from South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews with purposively sampled journalists and editors from these newsrooms. Findings show that the sceptical approach to AI adoption among Southern African community newspapers is largely driven by fears and concerns about AI’s documented mass production of misinformation and disinformation. In addition, the sceptical approach to AI adoption in these newsrooms is rooted in a lack of technical proficiency with AI tools and financial limitations occasioned by the decline in philanthropic funding.

articles.title: Algorithmic Silences: Postcolonial Blind Spots in Dutch AI Media Discourse
articles.authors: Jessy De Cooker, Adája Unlandt, Jessie Van Wijk
articles.abstract: The Kingdom of the Netherlands comprises four countries: the Netherlands, Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten, as well as three public entities located on the islands of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, and Saba. All these regions are former Dutch colonies and are located in the Global South. News coverage from former colonisers toward their former colonies is shaped by historical frameworks, political interests, evolving global power dynamics, and unequal news creation. This study specifically focuses on AI coverage in European-Dutch and Caribbean-Dutch newspapers, analysing 128 articles published between 2015 and 2025. By using a structured approach to analyse AI positioning, agency attribution, political-geographical framing, and epistemic visibility, this study develops a framework for examining and understanding how news media construct narratives along colonial lines. The analysis uncovers a structural imbalance: European-Dutch media rarely engage with AI developments in the Dutch Caribbean, producing what de Sousa Santos (2015) calls a “sociology of absences,” while Caribbean outlets frequently report on European-Dutch contexts and cite Dutch policymakers, institutions, and technologies. Across both media systems, AI is predominantly described as an externally produced technology, reinforcing Northern epistemic authority and positioning the Caribbean as a recipient rather than a co-producer of AI futures. These patterns reflect structural postcolonial inequalities within the Kingdom’s media ecosystem. The study highlights the need for more inclusive and locally informed reporting on AI to ensure that technological developments and societal implications in the Dutch Caribbean are part of the wider public debate.

articles.title: The Promise and Practice of Sharing Qualitative Data in Communication Research: Insights from the Qualitative Data Repository
articles.abstract: As open science ideas gain traction in communication and media studies, qualitative researchers face unique challenges and opportunities in adopting transparent and reproducible practices. This article contributes to the growing conversation on open research infrastructures by introducing the Qualitative Data Repository (QDR) as a domain-specific solution for qualitative and multi-method data sharing. QDR is particularly well-equipped to manage data derived from human participants or existing media materials, both of which are widely used in this field. We explore how QDR’s infrastructure, services, and ethical frameworks can be adapted to the needs of communication scholars. First, we briefly outline the benefits of qualitative data sharing—including increased transparency, methodological rigor, and pedagogical value—while acknowledging possible barriers such as ethical concerns, time constraints, and disciplinary histories. We then review practical developments that have taken place over the last five years by scholars practicing some of the principles for trustworthy qualitative communication research laid out by Humphreys et al. (2021). Using examples from a wide variety of projects where QDR has already facilitated data publication and annotations for transparent inquiry, we illustrate how similar practices can be adopted systematically in communication research. We also highlight QDR’s support for researchers throughout the data lifecycle, from planning and consent to curation and controlled access. This article aims to demystify qualitative data sharing and encourage broader adoption among communication and media studies scholars by showcasing QDR’s model and its alignment with findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable principles. We argue that embracing more open and transparent research practices not only enhances the quality and visibility of individual projects but also fosters a more inclusive and collaborative scholarly community.

articles.title: Navigating Online Visibility: Construction of Feminine Identity in Chinese Influencers’ Affective Networked Publics
articles.abstract: The rise of fashion and beauty influencers in China has produced highly visible representations of idealised femininity that increasingly appeal to young women and girls. This study examines how influencers on the Chinese social media platform Weibo discursively construct feminine identity through digital self-branding and how young women interpret and negotiate this mediated feminine visibility. By employing in-depth interviews with 31 Chinese urban young women and a feminist critical discourse analysis of 48 selected posts produced by leading female influencers, this study identifies three interrelated discursive resources through which idealised femininity is assembled: ambiguous feminism, an entrepreneurial beauty discourse, and aspirational consumption. Drawing on Berlant’s concept of intimate publics, the study argues that these discourses circulate affectively through relatability, producing both belonging and discipline within the community. Participants actively negotiate these representations through tactically extracting symbolic values and managing pressures to construct a legible feminine subjectivity. Furthermore, this study argues that asymmetric gendered power relations are reproduced through affective circulation within feminised digital spaces.

articles.title: Stratified Mobile Parenting Capital: Restrictive, Reformist and Radical Parenting Among Rural Migrant Working Families in China
articles.abstract: This study proposes the concept of mobile parenting capital, defined as the knowledge and capacities that parents draw upon to mobilise resources across spaces to support their parenting. Through interviews and observations with rural migrant worker parents, social workers and teachers in China, the study identifies three stratified parenting strategies: restrictive, reformist and radical. Restrictive parents possess limited digital resources and rely heavily on rural schools. Reformist parents actively employ digital tools to facilitate translocal parenting and support their left-behind children. Radical parents, who frequently relocate their children between rural hometowns and urban destinations, accumulate the highest levels of mobile parenting capital, while further mobilising resources from both urban and rural contexts digitally and physically.

articles.title: Feelings among friends and foes in populist communication: The Finns Party leadership’s emotional appeals on social media during the 2023 Finnish parliamentary election
articles.abstract: This study examines the use of emotional appeals in the social media communication by members of the populist radical right Finns Party leadership during the 2023 Finnish parliamentary election campaign. While previous research has highlighted the importance of emotions in populist communication, less empirical attention has been devoted to how populist radical right actors employ both negative and positive emotional appeals, how these appeals are directed toward different targets, and how their use varies across social media platforms. To address these gaps, we conducted a quantitative content analysis of 524 social media posts published on X (Twitter), TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram by six members of the Finns Party leadership. The findings show that negative emotional appeals are more prevalent and are primarily directed toward “elites” and “dangerous outgroups”, reinforcing a negative collective identity construction of antagonistic “others”. In contrast, positive emotional appeals are also used extensively and are primarily directed toward “the people” and populist actors as their representatives, reinforcing a positive collective identity construction of “us”. Finally, the analysis reveals variation across platforms, highlighting the need for further research on the relationship between social media platforms and emotional appeals.

articles.title: Vaccine framing dynamics: Media influence, social media sharing, and public sensemaking during a crisis
articles.abstract: During crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, information dissemination and sensemaking processes profoundly shape public perceptions. This study investigates the intricate interplay between media framing, social media sharing, and individual reinterpretation of COVID-19 vaccination news on Facebook. Analyzing 1957 articles from The New York Times (NYT) over 2 years, the research delves into news framing dynamics and their influence on Facebook sharing patterns. Findings reveal eight frames used by journalists, with a focus on scientific development, political controversy, and societal impact. Notably, the anti-vaccination frame received the highest number of shares per article. I also explored the content of the individual shares examining how individuals changed the information provided by the NYT during the sharing process.

articles.title: ‘Not for me’: Reasons for (non)participation in science communication activities on Artificial Intelligence in the Netherlands
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence operates in a social context and affects everyone. Organizing science communication and engagement activities on the topic for all groups in society is therefore recommendable. However, research shows that mainly higher educated, already engaged citizens participate in science communication activities. To address this gap, our study collected insights from underrepresented citizens in the Netherlands regarding their views on and participation in science communication activities related to artificial intelligence. Using semi-structured interviews (n = 19), we qualitatively explored reasons for (non)participation. Participants knew more about AI than they initially reported, and worldviews were evoked in expressing both concerns and curiosity about AI. AI was deemed relevant but news about the topic was avoided due to a lack of trust. Non participation in engagement or communication activity was driven by both practical and social barriers. Following participants’ advice, we suggest a personal approach could help to make these activities more inviting.

articles.title: Identifying Alternatives to Retraction of Controversial Research Findings
articles.authors: Mitch Brown, Donald F. Sacco, August Namuth, Cory J. Clark, Nathan Honeycutt
articles.abstract: Although academic journals have historically prioritized dissemination of accurate information, some journals now consider information hazards in editorial policies. Editors may reject or retract papers based on their perceived potential to impose societal harms. Such editorial policies have received pushback from scholars seeing such policies as impediments to effective science communication. Across four experiments, we tested how both scientists and everyday people view harm-based retractions and alternatives to retraction for addressing controversy. Academic researchers and lay perceivers disapproved of retractions based on information hazards, preferring commentaries, replications, adversarial collaborations, and even inaction . We offer policy recommendations for science communication.

articles.title: STEM Media Use and Interest Development in Childhood: A Research Note
articles.authors: J. Alex Bonus, Miriam Brinberg, Kate Stewart, Blue Lerner, Julia M. Wilson
articles.abstract: Can viewing educational videos through online streaming platforms (e.g., Netflix and YouTube) foster children’s interest in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM)? To address this question, parents ( N = 338) reported their 2- to 8-year-old children’s naturalistic STEM media use and STEM interests twice over a 1-month period. Children’s baseline STEM media use predicted an increase in their STEM interests over time, with a stronger relationship among older (vs. younger) children. These findings suggest that viewing STEM videos may serve as a catalyst for early STEM interest development, highlighting an important yet overlooked function of educational media use in childhood.

articles.title: Verifying Out of Alarm, or Alarmed After Verification? A Three-Wave Cross-Lagged Analysis of Multidimensional Risk Perceptions and Verification Behavior Amid Climate Misinformation in China
articles.authors: Liang Chen, Xiaoming Liu, Lunrui Fu
articles.abstract: Risk communication research often assumes that heightened risk perception drives subsequent behavioral responses, yet this perception-to-behavior logic remains underexamined. This study differentiates personal-level and societal-level risk perception and investigates their reciprocal associations with verification behavior in the context of climate change misinformation. Using three-wave panel data from China and cross-lagged structural equation modeling, results reveal a clear asymmetry: neither type of risk perception predicted subsequent verification. Instead, verification consistently increased societal risk perception over time, but not personal-level risk perception. These findings challenge the linear perception-to-behavior assumption and highlight a behavior-to-perception feedback pathway.

articles.title: Like Walking a Tightrope: User-Centric Perspectives on Content in Need of Moderation
articles.authors: Anna Maria Planitzer, Svenja Schäfer, Pia Pachinger, Sophie Lecheler
articles.abstract: Norm-violating content on social media platforms is on the rise, fueling prejudice and polarization. To counter such developments in a timely manner, platforms rely on automated content moderation. The issue, however, is that current understandings of automated moderation are mostly elite-driven, neglecting individual user perspectives, introducing biases and discrimination, and overlooking that users’ perspectives on what constitutes a norm violation in the first place may differ substantially from those of experts and platforms. Therefore, this study uses focus groups to explore what type of content users themselves think is in need of moderation. Findings suggest that users, while acknowledging the importance of moderating polarized topics (e.g., migration) and uncivil discourse styles (e.g., insults), are more concerned with the motivations of perpetrators and the vulnerability of targets. Our findings show that, if platforms want to incorporate user perspectives when designing automated moderation systems, they must move beyond merely detecting problematic message characteristics and focus on more tailored approaches, alongside accountability measures for perpetrators and safety measures for victims.

articles.title: Scrolling for the Truth: Source Factors, Persuasion, and a Test of Misinformation Interventions on TikTok
articles.authors: Brittany N. Shivers Weinstein, Bartosz W. Wojdynski
articles.abstract: The popularity of the video-based social media platform TikTok has rapidly grown in recent years, and with it its role in rapidly disseminating misinformation to its relatively young user base. However, little is known to date about how users perceive misinformation or about how platform interventions could be deployed to stop its spread. Two experiments examined users’ perceptions of TikTok videos making claims about a current health issue (monkeypox). Study 1 tested the impact of information type (true vs. false) and source (journalist vs. influencer) on users’ perceptions of TikTok videos, with party identification as a moderator. Participants rated message credibility and source quality higher for true videos and videos with a journalistic source. Study 2 tested the efficacy of three potential misinformation interventions (a banner label, pre-roll video, and click-through warning) and the role of psychological reactance. There was a main effect of the banner label and public service announcement pre-roll video on perceived message credibility. The interventions had no main effect on source quality, but there was a mediation of the PSA pre-roll and banner label on credibility and quality perceptions through reactance. In both studies, participants had difficulty discerning between true and false claims. Implications for journalists and social media companies are discussed, along with suggestions for future research.

articles.title: Skin Tone as a Visual Cue in Political Campaigns: Evidence from Elections in Mexico
articles.abstract: Research has long established that physical appearance and phenotypical traits influence how people evaluate political candidates. Skin color is one of the visual cues the electorate perceives during campaigns and media coverage, and a possible source of prejudice and bias. Here we use computational visual analysis to investigate the association between skin tone and electoral success during the 2024 Mexican Federal Elections. Our analyses incorporate important correlates not considered in prior research, most prominently news coverage, political ads, and social media use. We also account for geographic differences in average skin tone, explicitly modeling a source of variation that is obscured when skin tone is analyzed disregarding contextual baselines. We use fixed effects generalized linear models to control for state and party variation as well as candidate-level demographics, political experience, incumbency status, and media presence (news coverage, political ads, and social media use). Consistent with past work, we find that as candidates’ skin tone becomes darker, their predicted vote share declines. However, news coverage, political ads, and social media use are, together, more important predictors of electoral success than skin tone, indicating that this phenotypical trait is not as prominent a visual cue as earlier research suggested.

articles.title: Discursive village walls: (in)visible (in)formality in the semiotic loci of Gangxia Village, Shenzhen
articles.abstract: Amid the semiotic landscape of Chinese cities, urban villages are unique sites of text- and image-based communication and particular locales in which the modernizing city reveals itself. They took shape differently from the cities that sprawled around them when China’s cities began expanding. Their walls – surfaces – reflect their daily operations, overarching ordering system(s) and the negotiations between these two. This article researches the surfaces of Gangxia Village, an urban village in China’s youngest megacity, Shenzhen. Located beside the central business district (CBD), it is an example of a village that is increasingly acknowledged and regulated by municipal and district governments while remaining distinct. Following an expanded notion of urban informality and through the lens of visibility, the article engages geosemiotics as it surveys Gangxia’s walls, and the socio-spatial and visual negotiations registered on them. These walls display attempts at assimilation into the modern city alongside signs emerging from the village’s everyday operations. Beyond (within) the ‘semiotic landscape’, focusing on what could be called semiotic loci, the authors’ reading of the village manifests locationally specific versions of (in)visible (in)formality, positioning Gangxia as an (in)formal urban context embedded, through negotiations of (in)visibility, within the wider city.
